question: Explain overfitting to a manager who has no technical background.
reference_answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data too well, including the noise and the random mistakes. It is a bit like a student who memorises last year's exam answers. That student gets full marks on the old paper but fails when the questions change. In our case, the model looks very accurate on the data we used to build it, but it performs badly on new customers. To check for this, we keep part of the data aside and test the model on it. If the score on that test set is much lower, we simplify the model or collect more data.
key_phrases: memorise the answers; performs badly on new data; keep part of the data aside; test set; simplify the model

question: Walk me through how you would clean a messy dataset.
reference_answer: First I look at the data before I change anything. I check the shape, the column types and how many values are missing in each column. Then I look for duplicates and for values that make no sense, like a negative age or a date in the future. For missing values I decide case by case. If only a few rows are affected I may drop them. If a whole column is half empty I ask whether it is still useful. I also standardise text, for example making all city names use the same spelling. Finally I write every step in a script, so someone else can repeat the cleaning and get the same result.
key_phrases: check the column types; missing values; duplicates; case by case; standardise; repeat the cleaning

question: What is the difference between correlation and causation? Give an example.
reference_answer: Correlation means two things move together. Causation means one thing actually makes the other happen. A classic example is ice cream sales and drowning. In summer both go up, so they are correlated. But eating ice cream does not cause drowning. The hidden factor is hot weather, which makes people buy ice cream and also go swimming. In data science this matters because a model can find a strong correlation that is useless for decisions. If we want to know whether a change really causes an effect, we need an experiment, like an A/B test, or careful methods that control for other factors.
key_phrases: move together; hidden factor; confounding variable; A/B test; control for other factors

question: Describe a data project you are proud of. What was the problem and what did you find?

I used activity logs, quiz scores and login times from about two thousand students. After cleaning the data I tried logistic regression and a random forest. The random forest worked slightly better, but logistic regression was easier to explain, so we kept it. The strongest signal was simple: students who missed two weeks of logins in a row were much more likely to leave. The teachers then started sending a short message after one missed week.

question: How would you explain a p-value to a classmate who is confused about it?
reference_answer: I would say a p-value answers one specific question. If there were really no effect, how surprising would our data be? A small p-value, for example 0.01, means that data like ours would be rare if nothing was going on. So we start to doubt the idea of no effect. A p-value does not tell us the probability that our hypothesis is true, and it does not tell us how big or important the effect is. A tiny difference can have a small p-value if the sample is huge. That is why I always report the effect size and a confidence interval next to it.
key_phrases: if there were really no effect; how surprising; effect size; confidence interval; sample size

If we still disagree, I suggest we look at evidence, like data, a quick test or a user example, rather than opinions. If it is still not clear, we agree on who makes the final decision and I support it, even if it was not my idea. I think keeping a good relationship is worth more than winning one argument.

question: How do you politely interrupt someone in a meeting?
reference_answer: I usually wait for a small pause, then use a short phrase like 'Sorry to jump in' or 'Can I add something here?'. I keep my point short and connect it to what the person just said, so it does not sound like I am changing the topic. If someone keeps talking for a long time, I might say 'That is a good point, and I want to make sure we have time for the other items'. After I finish, I give the floor back: 'Sorry, please go on'. Body language helps too, like raising a hand slightly in online meetings.

question: What is RAG, and why do companies use it with language models?
reference_answer: RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. A language model only knows what was in its training data, and it can invent answers when it does not know. With RAG, before the model answers, the system searches a company's own documents and finds the most relevant pieces. Those pieces are added to the prompt, and the model answers using them. Companies like this because they do not need to retrain the model when documents change, they only update the search index. It also lets the system show the sources, so people can check the answer.
key_phrases: stands for; training data; most relevant pieces; added to the prompt; search index; show the sources

question: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chatbot?
reference_answer: A chatbot mainly answers messages. You ask, it replies, and the conversation is the whole product. An AI agent is given a goal and tools, and it decides the steps by itself. For example, an agent could read your emails, find a meeting time, check your calendar and send an invite. It plans, uses a tool, looks at the result, and decides the next step. That makes agents much more useful for real work, but also riskier, because a wrong step can have real effects. So good agents ask for permission before important actions.
key_phrases: given a goal and tools; decides the steps; looks at the result; riskier; ask for permission

So the simple parts of the job will take much less time. What stays hard is asking the right question, knowing whether the data can answer it, and explaining the result to people who make decisions. Those parts need context about the business and good communication. I think data scientists who use AI tools well will replace those who do not.

question: Explain how to cook a dish from your country.
reference_answer: I will explain how to make a simple Vietnamese noodle salad called bun thit nuong. While it cooks, boil rice vermicelli for a few minutes and rinse it in cold water. For the sauce, mix fish sauce, water, sugar, lime juice, garlic and chilli. question: What are the good and bad sides of tourism for a city?
reference_answer: Tourism brings money and jobs. Hotels, restaurants and small shops depend on visitors, and the income helps the city pay for transport and old buildings. It also makes local people proud of their culture. On the other side, too many tourists can push rents up, so local families move out of the centre. Some places become crowded and lose the feeling that made them special. I think cities should manage it, for example with tourist taxes or limits on short-term rentals, so the money stays and the problems stay small.
